evidence.finding: Routing configuration version 24.7 was deployed to all queues at 09:15, matching the incident start exactly.
Mean transfer rate rose from 6.22% before the incident to 12.52% afterward, a 101.46% increase beginning at 09:15.
Mean AHT increased from 378.0 seconds to 510.5 seconds (+35.0%); post-incident AHT was consistently about 34–39% above forecast.
Mean service level fell from 80.80% to 60.99% (-19.81 percentage points), while ASA rose from 38.1 to 63.8 seconds and answered calls declined 18.2%.
The routing-related processing shift was broad: all four queues showed AHT increases of about 35–38% and transfer-rate increases of about 88–117%; service-level impact varied by queue.
Scheduled and logged-in staffing remained constant at 49 agents; productive staffing changed only from 45.4 to 45.1 agents on average, and no agents were in training.
Mean offered volume decreased from 85.2 to 80.0 calls per interval after the incident, ruling out a center-level demand surge.

primary_root_cause_detail: Routing configuration version 24.7 was deployed across all queues at 09:15, exactly when transfer rates and AHT stepped up across the center. The resulting call-processing inefficiency reduced throughput and drove sustained service-level degradation despite stable staffing and non-surging demand.
recommended_actions: Roll back or correct routing configuration version 24.7 and validate destination, skill, and overflow rules before redeployment.
Monitor transfer rate, AHT, queue depth, ASA, and service level at 15-minute intervals after remediation, with queue-level checks for Account Support and General Service.
Add pre-deployment simulation and post-deployment guardrails that alert or automatically roll back when transfer rate or AHT changes materially across multiple queues.
Review transferred-call samples to identify the specific routing rules creating unnecessary handoffs.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Post-incident offered volume was 6.1% lower than pre-incident volume and averaged only 4.5% above forecast; the performance break was not demand-led.
Scheduled and logged-in agents stayed at 49 throughout, with only a negligible 0.7% reduction in mean productive staffing.
Mean adherence declined only 0.63 percentage points, insufficient to explain the abrupt, large deterioration.
No agents were in training during any visible interval.
Forecast AHT closely matched actual AHT before 09:15; the large AHT variance began precisely with the routing deployment, while post-incident volume variance was modest.

Staffed-agent counts were unchanged within every queue, while transfer-rate and AHT increases appeared across all queues, supporting a center-wide routing change rather than a primary capacity imbalance.
AHT was the immediate operational mechanism, but the deeper supported cause was the coincident all-queue routing deployment and associated doubling of transfers.
The only visible operational event was a routing deployment; no platform incident was recorded.

stakeholder_summary: The service-level incident was caused by the all-queue routing deployment at 09:15. Transfer rates approximately doubled and AHT rose 35%, reducing throughput and lowering mean service level by 19.8 percentage points. Demand and staffing remained broadly stable, so neither was a material driver.
